analysis.one_liner: Caps Medicare drug copays at the drug's post-rebate net price or its lower cash price.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in September 2025 with no cosponsors and referred to two House committees, where it has sat without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would limit what Medicare beneficiaries pay out of pocket for prescription drugs. For costs after the deductible but before reaching the annual out-of-pocket cap, a patient's cost-sharing could not exceed the drug's average net price (what the plan pays after rebates) or the pharmacy's cash price for an uninsured person, whichever is lower. The idea is to stop patients from being charged more than the drug actually costs once discounts are counted. Low-income Medicare enrollees' copays would also be capped at that amount, and the Government Accountability Office would report on compliance by 2029.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries, including the roughly 30 million enrolled in Part D drug plans, who would pay less at the pharmacy counter for drugs where current copays or coinsurance exceed what the plan actually nets after rebates, and low-income enrollees whose copays would also be capped at that amount.

how_it_helps.text: For drug costs after the deductible but before a beneficiary reaches the annual out-of-pocket threshold, cost-sharing for a month's supply could not exceed the drug's average net price after rebates, or the pharmacy's cash price, whichever is lower.
Low-income Medicare beneficiaries' copayments would also be capped at that same net-price amount starting in plan year 2027.
The Government Accountability Office would have to report to Congress by January 1, 2029 on whether plans comply and how enforcement could improve.

analysis.who_pays: Medicare drug plans, pharmacy benefit managers, and insurers would absorb the difference when post-rebate net prices are lower than the cost-sharing they currently charge; some of that cost could resurface in premiums or plan design.

drawbacks.text: The limit only applies after the deductible and before the out-of-pocket threshold, so beneficiaries still pay full price for the first fill(s) each year and the change does nothing before or after that band.

Plans might respond to the constraint by raising premiums or restricting which drugs are covered, shifting costs rather than eliminating them; the bill leaves that tradeoff unaddressed and relies on a GAO report in 2029 to flag problems.
It applies only to Medicare Part D drugs, not to private insurance, so most working-age people get no benefit.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit for Medicare enrollees could be real: linking what patients pay at the counter to what the drug actually nets after rebates would end a gap through which patients pay inflated middleman-set prices while insurers and pharmacy benefit managers keep the rebates. The drawbacks: implementation is complicated (plans' 'average net price' varies by drug and plan), it could complicate plan design or push plans to adjust premiums or formularies, and it only applies after the deductible, so patients with low drug costs see little change. As written it is a one-page mandate with a GAO check, and no committee has examined the mechanics.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees, which never acted on it, so it has no floor vote scheduled and sits in committee while Congress remains in session.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on September 8, 2025, and referred to the House Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees.
No other member signed on as a cosponsor.
Neither committee has taken it up, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote appears in the action history.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing has happened yet, so no one has gained or lost; Medicare drug plans and pharmacy benefit managers keep the current cost-sharing system as long as the bill sits in committee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nobody yet; drug plans keep status quo

for.name: Rep. Nicole Malliotakis
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to two committees.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's only support so far is a single Republican sponsor with no cosponsors from either party, so no partisan pattern has formed.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and Medicare drug plans
industries.note: Plans and the middlemen that set their drug prices could no longer set patient cost-sharing above a drug's post-rebate net price in the key coverage phase, shrinking the spread they can capture between what plans charge patients and what rebates bring in.

The bill does not directly cap what manufacturers charge, but by tying patient cost-sharing to net post-rebate prices it could increase pressure on rebate arrangements and make list-price games less useful to them.
Enrollees would pay at the counter no more than what the drug actually nets the plan after rebates, or the lower cash price, for most of each coverage year.

analysis.trajectory: Bills introduced late in a first session with zero cosponsors and dual committee referrals rarely advance; unless it attracts cosponsors or a committee hearing, it will likely die at the end of the 119th Congress without a vote.
